But it is now said that the nomination of the
Caucus at Washington should be supported to
sustain the party. Ave! The party!
What party? The Republican party? Surely
not. — This is the era of gouty feelings
"and nomination," is the order of the day.
The republicanism of James Monroe, like King Agrippa, is almost
persuaded, and James Monroe was compelled
to abandon it in relation to the National Bank;
the party in sustaining its principles has gone. And yet, we are
told that we should support the caucus nomina-
tion to sustain party "that has name to live
when dead." To sustain Wm. H. Crawford,
who eulogized the administration of John
Adams, to which the party is opposed, for its 'wisdom and firmness'—who open
abandoned its principles in the Senate of the
United States in the discussion on the charter of
the national bank; and who now constantly
conceals his opinions upon the great contested
questions of the day, which are supposed to
"The Party," to present the tests of political or
religious. And we are constantly told this too
by the very men who refused to come out last
winter in favour of the only true test of distinctions.
The wreck the remnant of that party who was
first in the nomination for the presidency of
these United States: was Nathaniel
Macon of North Carolina. A politician who
deserves to rank with Franklin and Taylor,
the Catos of Pennsylvania and Virginia. Does
not this incontrovertibly prove, that principles have
nothing to do in this contest about persons?

have been elected. What is the purpose then
of the contest of selection? Is the republi-

would say that Nathaniel Macon is not as con-

Queen Mary having dealt severely with the Protestants in England, about the latter end of her reign signed commission to take the same course in Ireland, and for that purpose nominated Dr. Cole, one of her commissioners. Cole coming to Chester, on his journey, was waited on by the mayor and in the magistrates presence took out of his bag, leather box, saying to him, here is commission that will lash the Protestants of Ireland. Coming to the council, after suitable speech, he presented the box to the lord deputy, Fitz Walters who ordered it to be opened that the secretary might read the commission but what was the surprise of the lord deputy, the council, and Dr. Cole, when the knave of Clubs and pack of cards appeared.
